holidays.name: A'Phabet Day (No "L" Day)
holidays.description: Today's wordplay holiday says that on Christmas Day you can sing "Noel" with the "L" taken out. Cheerful carolers can drop the L and belt out "No-e!" Alphabet fans and pun lovers get a seasonal reason to celebrate.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It plays on the "Noel" carol tradition and the idea that there is "no L" in the day.
holidays.funFact: The word "Noel" comes from the French word for Christmas, which traces back to the Latin word for "birth."

holidays.name: National Pumpkin Pie Day
holidays.description: Pumpkin pie gets a second turn on the table. It's a chance to eat spiced, creamy slices of the fall favorite after the big holiday feast. Whipped cream is strongly encouraged.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It follows pumpkin pie's long place on American holiday dessert tables.
holidays.funFact: Early colonial cooks often made pumpkin dessert by filling a hollowed-out pumpkin with milk, spices and honey, then baking it in hot ashes.

holidays.name: Grav Mass Day
holidays.description: A science-nerd twist on the holiday: a day to celebrate gravity and the scientist who explained it. Fans mark it with apples, physics jokes and a toast to Isaac Newton.
holidays.origin: The observance honors Isaac Newton, born on December 25, 1642, under the Julian calendar then used in England. The name is a pun on "Christmas" that swaps in "gravity."
holidays.funFact: Newton's birth date is December 25 only on the old Julian calendar. On the modern Gregorian calendar his birthday falls on January 4, 1643.
